blocks.text: devoured, miserably shrieking: not τιτίζοντας [titizontas], as Zenodotus wanted it read. Nor should anyone be surprised that Isaiah describes men chirping like birds. For it is a continuation of the metaphor. There the Prophet speaks in the words of the king of Assyria, who boasts like a Thraso and compares the peoples he has conquered with a nest of birds which fear of the fowler so dismays that they do not even dare to chirp. So the whole verse reads thus: And my hand has reached the wealth of the peoples as (birds') nest. And as one gathers abandoned eggs, I have gathered the whole earth; and there is none who moves a wing, or opens the mouth, or chirps. The words Καὶ ἀνοίγων στόμα, καὶ στρουθίζων [Kai anoigōn stoma, kai strouthizōn] [col. 150] are missing in most editions, and were read neither by Basil nor by Cyril. Yet the Complutensian edition and the recent Paris edition present them so. Theodoret also read them, and so did the Arabic translator, who made his version from the Greek. And in Procopius they are found in the margin with an asterisk. The version of the Elders, namely, is often rather free: provided they express the sense in some way, they are often little concerned about the words. Thus the Hebrew, And there is none who moves a wing, or opens the mouth, or chirps, they had rendered thus: Καὶ οὐκ ἔστιν ὃς διαφεύξεταί με, ἢ ἀντείπῃ μοί [Kai ouk estin hos diapheuxetai me, ē anteipē moi]: And there is none who escapes me, or contradicts me. But someone supplied the rest from another translator. Was it Aquila, who was most skilled in the Hebrew language and accustomed to render word for word?
The Arabic مصع [maṣʿ] matsaon for the male sparrow echoes the Dutch name of the sparrow, mosche, and the Norman moisson. Alcamus: المصع العصفور الذكرة [al-maṣʿ al-ʿuṣfūr al-dhakara].
